To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the ability of the restriction index to prevent change in the restricted trait depends on the number of loci affecting the trait and their mode of inheritance and on the initial allele frequencies and (2) in general, continued effectiveness is achieved only when the trait is affected by only one independent locus.
the ability to maintain a restriction depends on the number of loci affecting the restricted trait and on the genetic parameters of these loci.

the restriction of the genetic change in a trait is possible in the short term but difficult in the long term, and that the restriction of a trait is more effective when the genetic change is due to a single locus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) Can the genetic parameters of a population be changed by selection on a single trait, or by selection on several traits?
the development and application of methods for the estimation of the genetic parameters of traits in dairy cattle.
the effects of selection on genetic parameters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the restriction is not likely to be effective over several generations, unless the restricted trait is affected by one locus only.
the ability of a restricted index to maintain the restriction is very much dependent on the genetic parameters of the trait.

the ability of the index to restrict genetic changes in the restricted trait depends on: the number of loci affecting the trait; the number of locis affecting the trait and the correlated traits; the number of genes at each locus; the magnitude of the genetic effects; the genetic correlations between traits; and the gene frequencies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic change in the restricted trait was not always prevented, and the genetic change in a correlated trait was always allowed.
, in the case of two traits, the restricted index selection is effective only in the case of the independent loci.
it was not possible to maintain a restriction in the trait of interest for more than one generation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to consider the genetic architecture when developing restricted index selection schemes.
it is very difficult to maintain genetic change in one trait while preventing it in another.
genetic parameters can change over time, even under restricted index selection, which can affect the effectiveness of the restriction.
